lessons.title: MOCK - Reading a Small Data Table

steps.title: Goal and explanation
steps.body: MOCK ORIGINAL LESSON. A table organizes records as rows and attributes as columns. A primary key distinguishes each row and must be unique and present. Filtering selects matching rows; it does not rewrite the original table.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Consider rows (id=1, subject=computing), (id=2, subject=math), (id=3, subject=computing), (id=4, subject=art). The condition subject = computing selects rows 1 and 3, so COUNT(*) for that filtered set is 2. The table still has four stored rows.

steps.title: Guided check
steps.body: Apply the explanation, then inspect the corrective feedback.

steps.title: Explain the rule
steps.body: Read a condition one row at a time. Mark matching rows, then count those marks. COUNT(*) counts matching rows in this example, whereas reading a column value reports data from a row. A SELECT filter does not delete nonmatching rows.

steps.title: Trace the order
steps.body: Arrange the steps using the labeled movement controls.

steps.title: Independent application
steps.body: Use the rule in this new small example.

steps.title: Summary and later review
steps.body: Separate storage from a query result. A key identifies rows, a condition selects them, and a count reports how many matched. The original rows remain unchanged by this read-only selection.

questions.prompt: Which property is required of the id column when it is the primary key?

options.text: Every row has a unique, present id
options.feedback: This lets the key identify one row without ambiguity.

options.text: All rows share the same id
options.feedback: A shared value cannot distinguish one row from another.

options.text: The id may be absent for every row
options.feedback: An absent value cannot provide a primary-key identity.

questions.hint: A key should identify exactly one row.
questions.explanation: Uniqueness and presence are essential for primary-key identity; the values need not be consecutive.

questions.prompt: Order the demonstration operations for a new table.

options.text: Create the table with its column definitions
options.feedback: The table must exist before rows can be inserted.
Add rows before expecting the example query to find them.

options.text: Select rows whose subject is computing
options.feedback: Run the query after the example rows have been added.

questions.hint: Define storage, add data, then inspect it.
questions.explanation: This demonstration creates a structure, fills it, then reads matching rows. It makes no claim about concurrent database transactions.

questions.prompt: Rows have subjects computing, math, computing and art. How many satisfy subject = computing?
questions.hint: Count the two rows with the exact named subject.
questions.explanation: The first and third rows match. Two matching rows are returned; the stored table is unchanged.

questions.prompt: What two-word term names a column or column set used to identify each row uniquely?
questions.hint: It is the main key used for row identity.
questions.explanation: A primary key provides a unique, present identity for each row.

questions.prompt: Rows have ids 11, 12, 13 and 14. How many satisfy id > 12?
questions.hint: Only values strictly greater than 12 match.
questions.explanation: Ids 13 and 14 match, so the count is two.

glossary.definition: A named attribute represented across the rows of a table.
A unique, present column or column set that identifies a row.
A condition used to choose matching rows for a query result.
